data.cultural_impact: Ganesha, also known as Ganpati, Lord Ganesha, or Vinayak, is widely revered in the Hindu pantheon as the god of wisdom, knowledge, good fortune, and success. He is known to remove obstacles and bring good luck. The festival of Ganesh Chaturthi, celebrated in India and Nepal, is a major event in the Hindu calendar and is a time for community, family gatherings, and the display and worship of huge statue of Lord Ganesha.
data.spiritual_significance: Ganesha is believed to be the god who removes obstacles and grants success. In Hinduism, he is considered to be the god of knowledge and wisdom, the deity who symbolizes new beginnings and fresh starts. He is often invoked before embarking on new projects, initiatives, or even daily activities. Ganesha's elephant head represents his immense wisdom and power, and his broken tusk symbolizes the importance of breaking attachment and overcoming obstacles in the pursuit of knowledge and spiritual growth. Ganesha is also known as the god of Balance, remover of obstacles, and deva-guru or the teacher of gods and then the teacher of mankind. A spiritual and emotional bond is formed between the seeker and Lord Ganesha, as he is considered the first god to be invoked before starting any new venture or project.

historical_references.reference: Ganpati is believed to have been installed as the chief deity by Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, the founder of the Maratha Empire in the 17th century, during the construction of his new capital city, Raigad.
Another reference to Ganpati is found in the Mahabharata, where he is mentioned as the elder brother of Lord Keshava (Vishnu) and is known as Heramba or Herambha, the destroyer of obstacles.

modern_usage.modern_context: Ganpati, also known as Lord Ganesha, is a major deity in Hinduism and is revered as the god of wisdom, new beginnings, and obstacle remover. During the Ganesh Chaturthi festival, which is celebrated in late August or early September, millions of devotees install idols of Lord Ganesha in their homes and temples. These idols are often made of clay and are immersed in water after 10 days of worship. The festival is a time for community gatherings, family bonding, and expressions of devotion.
